matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export, the code executes arbitrary JavaScript via the gray-matter front matter parser, reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync, and injects the file contents into the CSS of the generated PDF, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code abuses the Markdown front matter feature to execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which is highly abnormal and dangerous. It directly accesses sensitive files using Node.js APIs and exposes their contents to the user through the generated PDF.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, Markdown-to-PDF conversion should only process markup and never execute arbitrary code. The expected behavior is safe, deterministic rendering of user input, not server-side code execution or file access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Server-side code execution via Markdown front matter is never legitimate in production environments. In rare, highly controlled admin-only scenarios, such features might be used for advanced templating, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input.
key_indicators: Presence of ---js front matter blocks in Markdown input
Arbitrary JavaScript execution during Markdown parsing
Direct filesystem access via require('fs').readFileSync in user-supplied content
Injection of sensitive file contents into user-facing output (PDF)
Lack of input sanitization or code execution restrictions in Markdown processing

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export

package_info.why_malicious: The md-to-pdf package (version 4.1.0) is critically vulnerable because it uses the gray-matter library with JavaScript engine support enabled by default. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary JavaScript code via Markdown front matter, resulting in remote code execution (RCE) on the server. Exploitation enables attackers to read sensitive files (such as /flag.txt) and exfiltrate their contents, violating core security boundaries.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits specially crafted Markdown containing a ---js front matter block with malicious JavaScript to the invoice generator.
attack_chain.leads_to: Server parses the Markdown and executes the embedded JavaScript code.

attack_chain.action: The malicious JavaScript reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data (flag) is loaded into memory during document generation.

attack_chain.action: The code injects the flag value into the CSS of the generated PDF document.
attack_chain.leads_to: Flag is exfiltrated to the attacker via the exported PDF file.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of arbitrary JavaScript during Markdown-to-PDF conversion
Access to sensitive files (e.g., /flag.txt) from within Markdown processing
User-controlled input leading to server-side code execution during document generation
file_indicators: Markdown files or input containing ---js front matter blocks
References to require('fs') or other Node.js modules in user-supplied Markdown content
network_indicators: Unusual outbound connections initiated during Markdown processing (if exfiltration is attempted via network)
No direct network indicators in this specific exploit, but possible in variants where exfiltration is performed over the network
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the use of ---js front matter in Markdown inputs, especially when processed by md-to-pdf or gray-matter. Audit application logs for unexpected file access (e.g., /flag.txt) during document generation. Use static analysis to detect unsafe use of gray-matter with JS engine enabled. Block or sanitize user-supplied front matter in Markdown, and upgrade md-to-pdf to a version that disables arbitrary code execution. Implement strict input validation and disable JavaScript execution in Markdown processing libraries.

package_info.why_malicious: A compromised version of the polyfill.io JavaScript library was served via CDN and injected malicious code into the Internet Archive website. This resulted in unauthorized modification of site content (defacement) visible to all visitors, and potentially enabled further browser-based attacks such as credential theft or data exfiltration. The attack violated the trust model of third-party libraries by executing malicious code in users' browsers.

attack_chain.action: The compromised polyfill.io JavaScript is served via the CDN and loaded by the Internet Archive website through a <script> tag.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious JavaScript is executed in the browser of every site visitor.

attack_chain.action: The malicious code executes in the user's browser, overwriting the DOM to display a defacement message.
attack_chain.leads_to: Site defacement is visible to all visitors; this also enables the attacker to potentially launch further browser-based attacks such as credential theft or data exfiltration if additional payloads are present.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected DOM manipulation (e.g., document.body.innerHTML or document.write) by third-party JavaScript libraries
Defacement messages or unauthorized content injected into page at runtime
Polyfill or utility libraries performing actions outside their intended scope, such as modifying visible page content
file_indicators: polyfill.min.js or similar polyfill.io scripts loaded from untrusted or compromised CDN URLs
Inline or external scripts modifying document.body.innerHTML or document.write with defacement or attack messages
network_indicators: Requests to polyfill.io CDN endpoints known to be compromised
Unusual script loads from third-party domains not previously used by the site, especially polyfill.io
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unexpected DOM changes initiated by third-party scripts, especially those loaded from polyfill.io or similar CDNs. Alert on any script that overwrites the main content of the page or injects defacement messages. Track and compare the content of externally loaded JavaScript libraries against known-good hashes. Block or alert on polyfill.io CDN usage if the domain is known to be compromised. Implement runtime monitoring to detect unauthorized DOM overwrites by scripts not owned by the site.

slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code accesses the DOM via document.querySelector to modify a specified container element by injecting styled copyright and branding HTML content including an embedded SVG logo linked to "https://www.modiphy.com", resulting in displaying a customized copyright notice with branding on the webpage.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a self-contained script that modifies a specified DOM container element to inject a styled copyright notice and branding with an embedded SVG logo linking to a legitimate domain (modiphy.com). It uses standard DOM APIs such as document.querySelector and style manipulation without any obfuscation, remote script loading, or attempts to hide its intent. Compared to the known malicious patterns, it does not perform misleading comments, inject remote scripts, overwrite the entire DOM, or impersonate brands maliciously. The behavior is consistent with legitimate UI branding and copyright display, with no indicators of data exfiltration, code injection, or system manipulation.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time and runtime, the code displays misleading comments and copyright banners to disguise its true purpose, attempting to pass as legitimate analytics code and evade detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of fake copyright banners and misleading comments referencing well-known brands is a deliberate social engineering tactic to mislead users and reviewers, and to obscure the package's malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not misrepresent their origin or function through deceptive comments or attributions to unrelated brands.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Open source code may include copyright banners, but not to mislead about the code's true origin, authorship, or purpose.
key_indicators: Fake copyright attribution to Twitter, Inc.
Misleading comments referencing StatCounter.com
Obfuscated code immediately following deceptive comments
Brand impersonation in code comments

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, on page load or script execution, the code injects external scripts into the page, including a deprecated version of Ionicons and a remote script (slim.js) hosted on jsDelivr, which itself contains the trojanized jQuery. This enables further malicious code execution and persistence by loading additional payloads from attacker-controlled sources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script injects remote code from attacker-controlled sources without user consent, using a misleading deprecation warning to disguise its activity and facilitate further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not inject remote scripts or downgrade libraries without explicit user action or clear documentation. Core libraries should not dynamically load external code from untrusted sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script injection is used in some legitimate plugin loaders, but not in core libraries or without user awareness and explicit opt-in.
key_indicators: Injection of remote scripts from suspicious or attacker-controlled domains
Phony deprecation warnings in console output to mislead users
Use of outdated or deprecated library versions

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a trojanized version of jQuery in which the 'end' prototype function is maliciously modified to exfiltrate all form data from the page to attacker-controlled domains whenever it is called, either directly or indirectly (e.g., via fadeTo). The package is distributed under many names and versions, often with additional suspicious files and unique exfiltration URLs, indicating a persistent, manually assembled supply chain attack targeting web applications.

attack_chain.action: User installs a malicious npm package containing a trojanized jQuery file (or similar).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is present in the project and loaded in the browser.

attack_chain.action: Trojanized jQuery is loaded and used in the web application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious prototype function (end) is available in the global jQuery object.

attack_chain.action: User or application code calls fadeTo or end (directly or indirectly), triggering the malicious end function.
attack_chain.leads_to: Form data is serialized and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled domains.

attack_chain.action: Injected scripts (from icons.js/min.js) load additional remote payloads (e.g., slim.js) from jsDelivr, which may contain further trojanized code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and further compromise of the web application.

Dynamic injection of remote scripts from non-standard or outdated sources
Presence of phony deprecation warnings in console output

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan JavaScript dependencies for modifications to core library prototype functions (e.g., jQuery.fn.end). Flag any code that serializes and exfiltrates form data to external domains. Monitor for dynamic script injection from non-standard or outdated sources, and alert on requests to known campaign domains. Review package contents for unexpected files (e.g., termux.properties, npm logs) and non-standard file naming patterns. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify supply chain attacks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Polyfill libraries are only expected to provide compatibility shims and should never modify visible page content or inject defacement messages. The presence of code that overwrites the DOM with a defacement message is a clear indicator of a supply chain compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate polyfill libraries do not alter the main page content or perform any DOM manipulation unrelated to feature shimming. The malicious code performs unauthorized, user-visible DOM overwrites.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate site banners or notifications may update the DOM, but this is always done by site-owned scripts, not by third-party polyfill libraries, and never to display defacement or attack messages.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code dynamically creates a <script> element, sets its source to a remote attacker-controlled domain (castleservices01.com), injects it into the DOM, and loads additional malicious JavaScript, resulting in the execution of a crypto drainer payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code injects a remote script from an untrusted, unrelated domain at import-time, which is a classic supply chain attack technique for delivering further malicious payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate animation library should not load or execute external scripts from domains outside its official infrastructure, especially not from suspicious or unrelated domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some analytics or feature flag services may load remote scripts, but only from trusted, well-known domains with transparent purposes.
key_indicators: Dynamic creation and injection of <script> elements

Script loading at import-time rather than user action

package_info.why_malicious: Versions 2.0.5, 2.0.6, and 2.0.7 of the lottie-player npm package were compromised in a supply chain attack. The attacker injected code that loads a remote crypto drainer script, which prompts users to connect their cryptocurrency wallets and then exfiltrates assets (cryptocurrency and NFTs) to attacker-controlled addresses. This malicious behavior is unrelated to the legitimate functionality of an animation library and poses a severe risk to users.

attack_chain.action: Malicious lottie-player package is loaded by the website (via CDN or npm), triggering the import-time execution of injected code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Loads remote drainer script from attacker-controlled domain (castleservices01.com).

attack_chain.action: The drainer script, once loaded, injects a wallet connect UI and prompts the user to connect their crypto wallet.
attack_chain.leads_to: User is deceived into connecting their wallet, granting access to wallet information.

attack_chain.action: Upon wallet connection, the script exfiltrates wallet information and initiates unauthorized transactions to steal assets.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim's cryptocurrency and NFTs are transferred to attacker-controlled addresses.

behavioral_signatures: Dynamic script injection from domains not affiliated with LottieFiles (e.g., castleservices01.com) during import-time of lottie-player.js
Wallet connect prompts or web3 wallet access requests on sites not expected to interact with cryptocurrency wallets
Outbound WebSocket or HTTP(S) connections to known phishing or drainer domains (e.g., castleservices01.com) following wallet connection
file_indicators: dist/lottie-player.js containing references to castleservices01.com or similar suspicious domains
Presence of dynamically injected <script> elements with src attributes pointing to external drainer payloads
Unexpected modifications or additions to lottie-player.js in npm package versions 2.0.5, 2.0.6, or 2.0.7
network_indicators: Any network connections (HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket) to castleservices01.com
Outbound requests to domains with a history of crypto phishing or drainer activity after loading animation libraries
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for external script loads initiated by lottie-player.js, especially from domains not associated with LottieFiles. Flag any wallet connect prompts or web3 wallet access requests on sites that do not provide crypto-related functionality. Detect and alert on outbound network connections to known drainer or phishing domains (such as castleservices01.com) after loading animation libraries. Use file integrity monitoring to detect unauthorized changes or suspicious references in npm package files, particularly in dist/lottie-player.js for the affected versions.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime in the browser, the injected code appends a script tag with src set to https://send.wagateway.pro/client.js?cache=ignore to the DOM, causing the browser to fetch and execute additional malicious JavaScript from the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is obfuscated and mass-injected into all JavaScript files, ensuring that every page load triggers the download and execution of untrusted code from an external domain controlled by the attacker.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate code should not inject remote scripts from unrelated or untrusted domains into all JavaScript files, especially using obfuscation and without user or developer consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic script loading is sometimes used for analytics or feature toggles, but not in an obfuscated, repository-wide, and externally controlled manner.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript injected into all *.js files
Dynamically creates a script tag with src pointing to send.wagateway.pro/client.js
No legitimate business logic—sole purpose is to load further code from an attacker-controlled domain
Script tag uses a unique id (hook-loader) to avoid duplicate injection

execution_context.file_location: assets/js/*.js (appended to the end of every JavaScript file in the repository)

attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to authenticate as the victim and push code to their repositories.

JavaScript code that dynamically injects script tags with src pointing to suspicious external domains

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified GitHub Actions workflows that serialize and POST secrets or variables to external domains. Scan for mass changes to JavaScript files, especially for obfuscated code that injects remote scripts from send.wagateway.pro. Detect client-side code that attaches event listeners to password forms and exfiltrates credentials. Flag any network traffic to send.wagateway.pro domains as a high-confidence indicator of compromise.
